title: Direct Debit and GIRO Bills: Who Owns Them in AP?
summary: Auto-debited bills leave the bank before anyone approves them. How to give direct debit and GIRO payments an owner, a review step and a clean ledger match.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Direct debit and GIRO bills are paid before anyone in AP approves them, so they quietly bypass bill approval, payment release and often budget checks. You cannot stop the debit, but you can give it an owner. Keep a mandate register with an expected amount and a named budget owner for every auto-debit, flag those vendors so their invoices never enter a payment run, route each invoice for review rather than release, match it to the bank debit, and investigate anything outside tolerance. The result is fewer duplicate payments, faster disputes and no unowned charges sitting in the ledger.


## Introduction


Most accounts payable controls assume a simple order of events: the invoice arrives, someone approves it, someone releases the payment, and the money leaves. Direct debits reverse that order. The money leaves first, the invoice arrives later, and sometimes it never arrives at all.


Finance directors we speak with describe the result in practical terms. There are bills where the supplier has already been set up to deduct automatically from the bank, yet the business still needs a workflow so that someone owns that deduction. Without it, auto-debits become the one category of spend that nobody approves, nobody codes deliberately and nobody reviews until the year-end audit or a budget variance forces the question.


This guide explains why direct debit and GIRO bills escape normal AP controls and how to bring them back in without trying to switch the debits off.


## What Is a Direct Debit?


**A direct debit is a payment that a supplier pulls from your bank account under a mandate you authorised in advance.** After the mandate is in place, the supplier initiates each collection and your bank pays it with no new instruction from you.


Direct debits exist in most banking markets under different names. In the United Kingdom they run through the[Bacs Direct Debit scheme](https://www.bacs.co.uk/) . In the United States, recurring pulls usually run as ACH debits governed by[Nacha](https://www.nacha.org/) . In Singapore, the equivalent is GIRO.


## What Is GIRO?


**GIRO is Singapore’s interbank direct debit and credit system.** A business authorises a billing organisation to debit its account, and payments are then collected automatically on each billing cycle. The[Association of Banks in Singapore](https://www.abs.org.sg/consumer-banking/giro) describes how GIRO arrangements are set up and managed through participating banks.


For businesses, GIRO is typically used for utilities, telecoms, insurance premiums, rent, statutory payments and other recurring obligations. It is convenient and it avoids late payment. It also means a meaningful share of operating spend can flow out of the bank without ever touching the AP approval process.


## Why Do Auto-Debited Bills Escape AP Controls?


The core problem is sequencing. Every standard control assumes it can act before payment. Auto-debits remove that assumption.


Standard AP control Normal bill Direct debit or GIRO bill


Bill approval Happens before payment Happens after payment, if at all


Payment release Approver decides when to pay Supplier decides when to collect


Budget check Spend is checked before commitment Spend is discovered after the fact


GL coding Coded at capture by AP or AI Often coded from the bank feed by guesswork


Duplicate check Payment run checks for prior payment Invoice may be paid again manually


Ownership Approver is accountable Often nobody is clearly accountable


Every row is a gap. Individually they look minor. Together they mean an entire category of spend runs on trust.


## What Goes Wrong When Nobody Owns a Direct Debit?


The failures are rarely dramatic. They are slow, cumulative and usually found late.


### Silent price increases


Recurring charges creep. A subscription moves up a tier, a utility tariff changes, an insurance premium renews higher. Because nobody compares each debit with an expected amount, the increase is simply absorbed.


### Duplicate payments


The invoice for a debited charge lands in the AP inbox like any other bill. Someone captures it, it is approved and it goes into the next payment run. The supplier is now paid twice, once by debit and once by transfer, and the credit sits on their side until somebody notices. Our guide to[preventing duplicate invoices and payments](https://peakflo.co/blog/prevent-duplicate-invoices-payments-accounts-payable) covers why this pattern is so common.


### Zombie mandates


A service ends, a lease is not renewed, an office closes, but the mandate is never cancelled. The supplier keeps collecting, or collects a final amount that nobody checks.


### Wrong entity, wrong account


In multi-entity groups, a mandate set up years ago may debit the wrong entity’s account, or the charge is coded to whichever entity’s bank feed it appears in rather than the entity that consumes the service.


### Budget surprises


Because auto-debits never pass a budget check, they show up only when actuals are compared with budget, by which point the spend has already happened.


Failure How it is usually discovered Typical delay Who should have caught it


Price increase Budget variance review Months Budget owner


Duplicate payment Supplier statement or audit Weeks to months AP


Zombie mandate Year-end account review Up to a year Budget owner


Wrong entity debited Intercompany reconciliation Weeks Finance


Unbudgeted spend Monthly management accounts One close cycle Budget owner


The[Association of Certified Fraud Examiners](https://www.acfe.com/) consistently identifies weak review of recurring and automatic disbursements as a contributor to undetected billing errors and fraud. Even where there is no wrongdoing, unowned spend is unmanaged spend.


## Why You Should Not Simply Cancel the Direct Debits


Faced with these risks, some teams try to move everything back to manual payment. That is usually a mistake.


Direct debits exist for good reasons. They prevent late fees and service interruptions on essential services, they reduce payment run volume, and many suppliers, especially utilities and statutory bodies, strongly prefer or require them. Pulling every one back into a manual process adds work and risk elsewhere.


The better answer is to accept that the payment cannot be gated and to control everything around it: who owns the mandate, what the charge should be, how the invoice is reviewed and how the debit is matched.


## How to Give Direct Debit and GIRO Bills an Owner


**Step 1: Build a mandate register.** List every active direct debit and GIRO mandate, entity by entity. Extract candidates from the last twelve months of bank statements, because recurring debits are easy to spot there even when nobody remembers setting them up.


**Step 2: Flag direct debit vendors at capture.** Mark these vendors in your AP system so their invoices are recognised as already paid. This single setting prevents most duplicate payments, because the bill never enters a payment run.


**Step 3: Route each invoice for review, not release.** The invoice still goes to an approver, but the action is a review: is this charge valid, correctly coded and within budget? The approver is usually the budget owner for that category, using the same rules as[category-based invoice approval routing](https://peakflo.co/blog/category-based-invoice-approval-routing) .


**Step 4: Match each invoice to its bank debit.** Link the bill to the corresponding bank line so the payment entry is created from evidence, not assumed. The same principle applies to manual payments, as explained in our guide to[proof of payment for manually paid vendors](https://peakflo.co/blog/proof-of-payment-manual-vendor-payments-multiple-banks) .


**Step 5: Check variance against the expected amount.** Compare each debit with the register. Within tolerance, it flows through. Outside tolerance, it goes to the owner with both the invoice and the bank line attached.


**Step 6: Review mandates on a fixed cycle.** At least annually, ask each owner to confirm that each mandate is still needed. Cancel anything that is not.


## What Should a Mandate Register Contain?


Field Purpose Owner


Vendor and mandate reference Identifies the arrangement with the bank Finance


Entity and bank account debited Prevents wrong-entity charges Finance


Expected frequency Detects missed or extra collections Finance


Expected amount or range Detects price changes Budget owner


GL account and cost centre Codes the bill consistently Finance


Budget owner The person accountable for the spend Business


Contract end or renewal date Prompts review before renewal Budget owner


Last reviewed date Shows the mandate is actively managed Finance


The register does not need to be complicated. What matters is that it exists, that every mandate has an owner and that the expected amount is written down somewhere a system can compare against.


## Handling the Common Exceptions


Even with a register, three exceptions recur. Each needs a defined path rather than ad hoc handling.


Exception What it means Recommended handling


Debit with no invoice Supplier collected but sent nothing Create a placeholder bill, request the invoice, escalate after a set number of days


Invoice with no debit Supplier billed but has not collected yet Hold as expected debit, check the next bank feed, never release for manual payment


Debit outside tolerance Amount differs from expectation Route to owner with invoice and bank line, dispute or update the register


The middle case is the one that causes duplicate payments. An invoice that arrives before its debit looks like any other unpaid bill. If the vendor is flagged as direct debit, the system holds it rather than offering it for payment.


## Coding Auto-Debits Correctly


When nobody reviews direct debits, they tend to be coded from the bank feed, by whoever happens to be reconciling that week, using the description the bank provides. That produces inconsistent coding across months and entities.


Capturing the invoice and coding it through the same AI-assisted process as every other bill fixes this. The vendor history and mandate register supply the GL account and cost centre, and the review step lets the budget owner confirm it. The result is the same coding quality as[non-PO invoice processing](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/non-po-invoice-processing) for spend that previously bypassed it.

## What Metrics Show Auto-Debits Are Under Control?


Metric What it reveals Healthy direction


Debits with no matching invoice Charges nobody has reviewed Near zero beyond the agreed window


Debits outside tolerance Price changes and errors Small, each with a resolution


Duplicate payments to direct debit vendors Whether the paid-by-debit flag works Zero


Mandates without a named owner Gaps in accountability Zero


Mandates not reviewed in twelve months Risk of zombie mandates Zero


The[AICPA and CIMA](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/) emphasise in their management accounting guidance that controls should be measurable. These five numbers give a finance lead a monthly view of whether auto-debited spend is actually managed.


## Our Verdict: Is It Worth Building a Workflow for Direct Debits?


After reviewing how multi-entity finance teams handle auto-debits, our view is clear: the effort is small and the control benefit is significant.


### Build a direct debit workflow now if


- More than a handful of suppliers collect by direct debit or GIRO
- You have found duplicate payments to a debited supplier in the past year
- Budget owners are surprised by recurring charges in management accounts
- You operate several entities with different bank accounts
- Nobody can say who approves auto-debited bills today


### A lighter approach may be enough if


- You have only a few fixed-amount debits, such as rent, that never vary
- A single person reconciles every bank account and knows each debit personally


**Our Recommendation** : Start with the mandate register and the paid-by-debit flag. Those two steps alone eliminate most duplicate payments and give every debit an owner. Then add review routing and variance checks so that price changes and invalid charges are caught in days rather than at year-end.


## Conclusion


Direct debit and GIRO payments are not going away, and they should not. They prevent late fees and simplify payment for essential services. But they invert the order that most AP controls rely on, and that inversion creates a category of spend nobody owns.


You cannot approve a payment that has already happened. You can make sure someone is accountable for it, that the charge is checked against what it should be, that the invoice is never paid a second time and that the debit is matched cleanly in the ledger. That turns auto-debits from a blind spot into one of the most predictable parts of your payables.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**What is a direct debit?** A direct debit is a payment that the supplier pulls from your bank account under a mandate you signed in advance. Once the mandate exists, the supplier initiates each collection and your bank pays it without a new instruction from you.


**What is GIRO in Singapore?** GIRO is Singapore’s interbank direct debit and credit system, operated through the participating banks. Businesses commonly use it to pay utilities, telecoms, insurance premiums, rent, taxes and other recurring bills by authorising the billing organisation to debit their account.


**Why are direct debit bills hard to control in accounts payable?** Because the payment happens before, or without, the normal AP approval. The money has already left the bank when the invoice arrives, so the usual bill approval and payment release steps are skipped and nobody is clearly accountable for checking the charge.


**Should direct debit invoices still go through approval?** Yes, but as a review rather than a gate. The approval cannot stop the payment, but it confirms the charge is valid, correctly coded and within budget, and it gives a named owner the job of disputing anything wrong.


**How do you avoid paying a direct debit invoice twice?** Flag the vendor or the bill as paid by direct debit at capture so it is excluded from payment runs, and match it to the bank debit rather than releasing it for payment. Duplicate payments usually happen when someone pays the invoice manually without realising it was already debited.


**Who should own a direct debit mandate?** The budget owner for the spend category, not finance alone. Finance maintains the mandate register and the matching, but the business owner is accountable for whether the service is still needed and whether the charge is correct.


**What should a direct debit mandate register contain?** Vendor, entity, bank account debited, mandate reference, expected frequency, expected amount or range, GL account, budget owner, contract end date and the date the mandate was last reviewed.


**How do you catch price increases on recurring direct debits?** Compare every debit against the expected amount or range in the mandate register and route anything outside tolerance to the owner for review. Without an expected amount, small increases are absorbed silently.


**What happens if a direct debit arrives with no invoice?** Treat it as an exception with an owner and an age clock. Request the invoice from the vendor, and if none arrives within the agreed window, escalate, because the charge may be invalid or the vendor may have changed terms.


**Can direct debit bills be reconciled automatically?** Yes. When each debit is linked to a bill marked as paid by direct debit, the ledger payment entry can be created from the bank line and matched automatically, leaving only out-of-tolerance amounts and missing invoices for review.
